design_detail: Systematic review with dose–response meta-analysis of 17 observational studies (14 cohort, 3 case–control; published 1980–2003) of average alcohol intake and liver cirrhosis, analysed separately for women and men and for the two end-points, morbidity (clinically assessed) and mortality (death certificates). Random-effects meta-regression using the Greenland–Longnecker method for trend estimation (GLST procedure, Stata 10.1), with intake modelled two ways: first-degree fractional polynomials forced to be monotonic, and a categorical model with six intake categories (>0–12, >12–24, >24–36, >36–48, >48–60 and >60 g a day) against abstention. The reference group is lifetime abstainers: estimates from studies that used current abstainers were converted with a pooled relative risk for former drinkers. No protocol and no risk-of-bias appraisal of the primary studies. The stated purpose was to supply cirrhosis relative risks to the Comparative Risk Assessment for alcohol in the Global Burden of Disease 2005 study (p. 438).
can_establish: The average shape and size of the published association between average daily intake and the relative risk of liver cirrhosis up to January 2008, by sex and by end-point, relative to lifetime abstainers, and how much the morbidity and mortality studies differ from each other.
cannot_establish: That drinking causes the differences between intake categories beyond what the underlying observational studies can show (no study was appraised for confounding or bias); that alcohol affects death from cirrhosis more than the onset of cirrhosis (the end-point comparison is between different sets of studies, which also differ in design and country); that women are more susceptible than men (no test of the sex difference, and each sex's relative risk is against its own abstainers); whether low intake is safe for the liver (the categories below two drinks a day give contradictory estimates, including a significantly lower risk in men); or absolute risks (none reported).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Database search of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CINAHL, PsychINFO, ETOH and Google Scholar from January 1980 to January 2008, with key words for alcohol, alcohol consumption, alcohol intake, heavy drinking, liver diseases and liver cirrhosis, plus hand-searching of the content pages of major epidemiological journals and the reference lists of relevant articles and reviews; no language restriction (Methods › Literature search, p. 438). The included studies are general-population or occupational cohorts (for example Kaiser-Permanente, Framingham, American Cancer Society, Japanese physicians, Shanghai men) and three Italian case–control studies of liver disease (Table 1, p. 440; reference list, pp. 444–445).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cohort or case–control design; hazard ratios, relative risks or odds ratios with 95% CIs, or the information to compute them; end-point liver cirrhosis morbidity (clinical assessment) or mortality (death certificates), self-reports not accepted; three or more intake categories, one of them abstention. ICD codes considered: 581 (ICD-7), 571 (ICD-8 and ICD-9), K70 and K74 (ICD-10); no ICD-10 study was found. Excluded: reports not published in full (conference abstracts, letters to editors), cross-sectional designs, studies reporting intake only as a continuous measure or in two categories. Where a cohort had several reports, the one with the most comprehensive alcohol data was used (Methods › Case definition and Inclusion and exclusion criteria, pp. 438–439).
sample.demographics: Nine studies from the USA, four from Italy, two from Denmark, one each from Japan and China. Seven reported women and men separately, two women only, five men only and three both sexes combined (Results › Characteristics of the included studies, p. 440). Study sizes range from 369 to 548,185 participants and from 15 to 611 cases; the largest are Garfinkel et al. (1988; 548,185 women), Thun et al. (1997; 457,423) and Boffetta and Garfinkel (1990; 239,462 men) (Table 1, p. 440). Ages, follow-up and settings are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within primary studies is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Only studies that reported at least three intake categories including abstention were eligible, so studies reporting intake only continuously or in two categories were lost. The search began in 1980 and excluded conference abstracts and letters without a stated reason. The end-point comparison is confounded by study type: all four morbidity-only studies are Italian (three case–control studies and one cohort), the two studies with both end-points are Danish cohorts, and all eleven mortality-only studies are cohorts, nine of them American (Table 1, p. 440). Three American cohorts (Garfinkel 1988, Boffetta and Garfinkel 1990, Thun 1997) contribute 1625 of the 3384 cases (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used, converted by the reviewers to grams of pure alcohol a day using the type of beverage and the country's standard drink size, taken from the WHO International Guide for Monitoring Alcohol Consumption and Related Harm or an ICAP overview where a standard drink was not 12 g. Category ranges were represented by their midpoint; for an open top category, 75% of the width of the previous category was added to its lower bound (Methods › Standardisation of alcohol consumption, p. 439). Baseline intake in cohort studies is taken as an indicator of drinking over time (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph, p. 443).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average volume only, in grams of pure alcohol a day; the text equates one drink with 12 g (for example five drinks with 60 g, p. 438, and 'one to two drinks' with the >12–24 g category, p. 441). Categories: 0 (reference), >0–12, >12–24, >24–36, >36–48, >48–60 and >60 g a day (Methods › Statistical analysis, p. 439). Drinking pattern (binge drinking, drinking over time) and beverage type could not be analysed because the included studies lacked the information (Strengths and limitations, 4th paragraph, p. 443).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level. Tobacco, viral hepatitis and other drug use enter only through whatever adjustment each primary study made; which adjustments were made was extracted but is not reported (Methods › Data extraction, p. 439).

comparison.controls: Lifetime abstainers of the same sex (Table 2 footnotes, p. 442). For studies that reported risks only against current abstainers, the reviewers pooled the relative risk of former drinkers against lifetime abstainers from the studies that reported both, estimated the ratio of former drinkers to lifetime abstainers, and adjusted each such study's relative risks to a lifetime-abstainer reference, to avoid the sick-quitter effect (Methods › Data extraction, 1st paragraph, p. 439). The pooled former-drinker relative risk, the ratio and the number of studies adjusted are not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed: no appraisal of how the primary studies handled confounders (hepatitis B and C, obesity, smoking, socioeconomic position) or measurement of intake over time. The discussion argues that lifetime abstainers should be combined with very light, infrequent drinkers as the reference group (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 442), but the analysis does not do this.

outcomes.instruments: Liver cirrhosis morbidity by clinical assessment and cirrhosis mortality by death certificate, coded by ICD-7 581, ICD-8 and ICD-9 571, or ICD-10 K70 and K74 (Methods › Case definition, p. 438). The outcome is cirrhosis of any cause as coded, not alcoholic cirrhosis alone.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed. The reviewers argue on biological grounds that alcohol should affect mortality more than morbidity, because drinking worsens existing liver disease and impairs immunity (Introduction, 4th paragraph, p. 438).
outcomes.operationalization: Relative risk of cirrhosis morbidity or mortality at each intake level against lifetime abstainers, by sex; odds ratios, relative risks and hazard ratios were all treated as relative risks (Methods › Data extraction, p. 439).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 24 counts the categorical estimates in Table 2 (six intake categories × two end-points × two sexes), each with its own P value, plus 12 mortality-versus-morbidity interaction P values; the continuous models add two fractional-polynomial fits and two interaction tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Extraction was done independently by two investigators; a third investigator re-extracted a random sample of 15 articles and agreed on 95.6% of 710 data points (Methods › Data extraction, p. 439). Whether screening was done in duplicate is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: All relative to lifetime abstainers of the same sex; intake in grams of pure alcohol a day (one drink = 12 g). Categorical random-effects model (Table 2, p. 442). Women, mortality: >0–12 g 1.9 (95% CI 1.1–3.1); >12–24 g 5.6 (4.5–6.9); >24–36 g 7.7 (6.3–9.5); >36–48 g 10.1 (7.5–13.5); >48–60 g 14.7 (11.0–19.6); >60 g 22.7 (17.2–30.1). Women, morbidity: 0.4 (0.1–1.2); 1.0 (0.5–1.9); 2.4 (1.8–3.2); 1.9 (1.4–2.6); 5.9 (3.7–9.3); 6.1 (4.6–8.0). Men, mortality: 1.0 (0.6–1.6); 1.6 (1.4–2.0); 2.8 (2.3–3.4); 5.6 (4.5–7.0); 7.0 (5.8–8.5); 14 (11.7–16.7). Men, morbidity: 0.3 (0.1–0.9); 0.3 (0.2–0.4); 0.7 (0.5–1.0); 2.0 (1.5–2.7); 2.3 (1.7–3.2); 5.0 (3.9–6.4). Continuous (fractional polynomial) model: best fit power 0.5 in women (deviance 76.12 lower than the linear model) and linear in men; for women, mortality RR 4.9 (4.0–6.2) at 24 g and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g a day, morbidity 3.2 (2.6–3.9) and 6.2 (4.4–8.7) (Results › Dose–response meta-analyses, pp. 441). Heterogeneity in the continuous models: women Q = 200.59, I² 72% (63–78%); men Q = 305.22, I² 78% (72–82%). Dose × end-point interaction: women χ² 7.89, 1 df, P = 0.005; men χ² 17.06, 1 df, P ≤ 0.001. No absolute risks.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Primary-study adjustments were extracted but are not reported, and the paper does not say whether the most-adjusted estimate of each study was used. End-point (mortality or morbidity) entered the continuous model as an interaction with dose.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The continuous-model estimates are given in the text only for women at 24 and 60 g a day; men's values and all curves (Figure 2) are shown without intervals. The sensitivity analysis restricting to studies with sex- and end-point-specific results is described as giving a very similar pattern, with no numbers (p. 442). Residual heterogeneity after adding end-point to the model, and heterogeneity in the categorical model, are not reported. The significantly lower morbidity risks in men drinking up to 36 g a day appear in the results and limitations but not in the abstract. Table 2 gives no number of studies, datasets or cases behind any cell (p. 442).
analysis.power: Not discussed. The morbidity estimates rest on six studies (four Italian, two Danish) in each sex; Egger and Begg tests on 12 and 15 datasets have limited power to detect small-study effects (editors' observation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 17 mostly American and Italian studies, the relative risk of cirrhosis rose steeply with average intake in both sexes and both end-points, reaching 14 to 22.7 for death and 5.0 to 6.1 for morbidity above 60 g a day against lifetime abstainers. Mortality studies gave larger relative risks than morbidity studies at every level. Below about two drinks a day the estimates diverge: women in mortality studies already had a raised risk at up to 12 g a day (1.9), while men in morbidity studies had significantly lower risks than lifetime abstainers up to 36 g a day (0.3, 0.3, 0.7), and women's morbidity risk was not raised up to 24 g a day and was lower at 36–48 g than at 24–36 g. Women's relative risks exceeded men's at the same intake, without a formal test.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports "some indications for threshold effects" and a significantly larger effect of alcohol on mortality than on morbidity (p. 437), and the conclusions call the biological hypothesis for this "confirmed" (p. 443). Gaps: (1) the mortality–morbidity contrast is a comparison between two sets of studies that also differ in design (case–control against cohort) and country (Italy and Denmark against mainly the USA), and the same data were entered in both sets when a study did not separate end-points, so it cannot confirm a biological mechanism; (2) the 'threshold' for morbidity includes significantly lower risks in men drinking up to three drinks a day, which the authors themselves call a protective effect without a biological pathway (p. 443) and which suggests a problem with the reference groups of the morbidity studies, but the abstract does not mention it; (3) the statement that women have a higher risk at the same intake compares relative risks against each sex's own abstainers, without a test; (4) the public-health advice that no drinking can be recommended where cirrhosis is concerned and that people with any liver problem should abstain (p. 442) goes beyond the data, which concern average intake in general populations. The discussion does caution that the pooled estimates should be read in the light of the primary studies' limitations (p. 442).

timeline.event: English et al., an Australian report on drug-caused morbidity and mortality (this review's ref 8): more than ninefold risk of cirrhosis above 40 g a day in both sexes against abstainers, so no sex difference in relative risk at heavy intake, though risks differed between women and men at 20–40 g a day (as summarised in this review's introduction, p. 438).

Corrao et al., meta-analyses of 1998, 1999 and 2004 (this review's refs 5–7): a continuous, almost exponential rise in cirrhosis risk without an evident threshold, a significant increase from 25 g a day against abstainers, and high heterogeneity that this review suspected came from the end-point (Introduction, pp. 437–438).

Kamper-Jørgensen et al. (Danish cohort, J Hepatol): a threshold above about five drinks (60 g) a day, with 27-fold (men) and 35-fold (women) mortality from alcoholic cirrhosis against the Danish general population, and no further dose–response, as summarised in this review's introduction (p. 438).
Rehm et al. (Lancet), the global burden estimate cited here for about 15% of alcohol-attributable deaths in 2004 being due to cirrhosis (p. 437).
This review; its relative risks were intended for the Comparative Risk Assessment for alcohol in the Global Burden of Disease 2005 study (p. 438).

Askgaard et al., Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort: cites this review for a raised alcoholic-cirrhosis risk at one to two drinks a day, which holds for the review's mortality estimates but not its morbidity estimates, and notes the review's different morbidity and mortality risk functions; deaths were only 11% of its cases, too few to compare the end-points (card sc_askgaard_2015).

Roerecke et al. (Am J Gastroenterol), dose–response meta-analysis of alcohol and cirrhosis with sex differences, the update listed on the round's Tier A evidence map (card sc_roerecke_2019). Six of its nine studies are among the 17 here (Garfinkel et al., 1988; Boffetta and Garfinkel, 1990; Fuchs et al., 1995; Klatsky et al., 2003; Corrao et al., 1993 and 1997), so the two reviews are not independent.

replication.where_it_stands: The steep rise of cirrhosis risk with average intake is consistent with the earlier Corrao meta-analyses it updates. Its two distinctive claims, a larger relative risk for cirrhosis death than for cirrhosis onset and a threshold for morbidity, rest on between-study contrasts in four Italian and two Danish morbidity datasets and should be checked against the 2019 update (Roerecke et al.) before a claim relies on them. Two Danish cohorts (Becker et al., 1996 and 2002) are among its 17 studies; the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort (Askgaard et al., 2015) is not, so the two can be cited together without double counting.

funding.funder: NIAAA (contract HHSN267200700041C, 'Alcohol- and Drug-Attributable Burden of Disease and Injury in the US', to the first author) and the Global Burden of Disease and Injury 2005 Project provided financial and/or technical support; the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long Term Care supports salaries and infrastructure at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Acknowledgements, p. 443).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All seven authors are at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto (the first author also at the University of Toronto and TU Dresden). The review was done to supply relative risks to the alcohol Comparative Risk Assessment of the Global Burden of Disease 2005 study, whose core group is thanked for comments (p. 443), and its introduction cites the first author's global burden paper (Rehm et al., 2009). No author is an author of an included study. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A dose–response meta-analysis of individual-participant data from prospective cohorts that record both incident cirrhosis (hospital records) and cirrhosis death (death registers) in the same people, with lifetime abstainers separated from former and occasional drinkers and with absolute incidence by sex, so that the morbidity–mortality and sex comparisons are made within cohorts rather than between different kinds of study.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Exposure (average intake in at least three categories including abstention), comparator (abstention, converted to lifetime abstention), outcomes (cirrhosis morbidity by clinical assessment and mortality by death certificate, with ICD codes) and designs are specified (pp. 438–439).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Cohort and case–control studies were chosen as giving stronger control than cross-sectional studies (Inclusion and exclusion criteria, pp. 438–439).

Seven databases including Google Scholar, key words given, hand-searching of journal content pages and reference lists, no language restriction (p. 438); but the search was limited to 1980 onwards and reports not published in full (conference abstracts, letters) were excluded, without a stated reason; no study registries or experts consulted. Applied as written (decision p-amstar2-item4); a lenient reading would give partial yes. The search ended in January 2008, about two and a half years before publication.
Who screened records and assessed eligibility, and whether two people did, is not stated; only extraction is described as duplicate.
Independent extraction by two investigators, with a third re-extracting a random sample of 15 articles (95.6% agreement on 710 data points) (p. 439).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives only numbers excluded (109 after screening articles, 41 after applying the inclusion criteria), without a list or reasons (p. 440).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives author, country, sex, design, cases, sample size and end-point (p. 440). The exposure measure and categories, the reference group used (current or lifetime abstainers), covariates, ages, setting and follow-up are not described for any study, so the five elements needed even for partial yes are not all present.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal of the included studies. The conversion of current-abstainer references to lifetime abstention addresses one bias (sick quitters) analytically but is not a study-level assessment, and confounding is not assessed at all.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects dose–response meta-regression with Greenland–Longnecker trend estimation is an appropriate technique (p. 439), but the paper does not say that adjusted estimates were combined; odds ratios, relative risks and hazard ratios are pooled as one measure; results reported for both sexes combined were entered in both sexes' datasets, and results combined across end-points in both end-point datasets, so the same data appear twice (p. 439); and current-abstainer references were converted with an unreported pooled former-drinker relative risk.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, so no analysis of its impact; the only sensitivity analysis concerns studies without sex- or end-point-specific results and is reported without numbers (p. 442).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: One general sentence asks readers to interpret the estimates in the light of the primary studies' strengths and limitations (p. 442); the interpretation of the mortality–morbidity difference and of the thresholds does not consider bias in the primary studies.

Q and I² with confidence intervals are reported for the continuous models (p. 441), and end-point and sex were examined as sources of heterogeneity and discussed; residual heterogeneity after adding end-point is not reported.

Begg–Mazumdar and Egger tests in each sex (women P = 0.837 and 0.215; men 0.767 and 0.196) and a discussion of publication bias (pp. 440–441, 443); the funnel plots are not shown and the tests have limited power with 12 and 15 datasets.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding is reported in the acknowledgements, but there is no conflict-of-interest statement and no description of how conflicts were managed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six of the seven critical items are not met (2, protocol; 4, unjustified limits on date and publication type; 7, excluded studies; 9, risk of bias of included studies; 11, pooling of unstated adjusted estimates with data entered twice; 13, bias not considered in interpretation); only item 15 is met. Under AMSTAR 2 this gives critically low confidence, and it would do so under the lenient reading of item 4 as well. The review is useful as a quantitative summary of the cirrhosis dose–response in published studies to 2008, kept apart by sex and end-point and referenced to lifetime abstainers; its numbers can be cited as what these 17 studies show, relative to lifetime abstainers, with the steep rise at higher intakes as its most robust result. It cannot be cited on its own for a safe threshold, for a biological difference between cirrhosis onset and death, for a protective effect of light drinking in men, or for greater female susceptibility.

key_findings.finding: Selection: 3,238 records, 167 left after screening abstracts for liver cirrhosis, 58 articles assessed against the inclusion criteria and 17 studies included (14 cohort, 3 case–control; mortality end-point 11, morbidity 4, both 2); 109 and 41 articles were excluded at the last two steps, without reasons.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (flow diagram); Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The numbers are printed inside the Figure 1 image and are not in the text extraction; they were read on the rendered page.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Figure 1 read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: The 17 studies (published 1980–2003; 9 USA, 4 Italy, 2 Denmark, 1 Japan, 1 China) provided 12 datasets for women and 15 for men, with 1 477 887 participants and 3384 cases of cirrhosis in total; seven reported women and men separately, two women only, five men only and three both sexes combined.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The total is printed as 1477 887. Editors' check: the sample sizes and case counts in Table 1 sum to the totals in the text (1,477,887 and 3384). The three studies without sex breakdown entered both sexes' datasets (p. 439), which is why 12 + 15 datasets come from 17 studies.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Methods that shape every estimate: search of seven databases from January 1980 to January 2008 without language restriction; intake converted to grams a day using each country's standard drink (12 g as the base), category midpoints, and for open top categories the lower bound plus 75% of the previous category's width; current-abstainer references converted to lifetime abstention with a pooled former-drinker relative risk; results combined across sexes or end-points entered in both datasets.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Literature search (p. 438); Data extraction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Standardisation of alcohol consumption (p. 439)
key_findings.note: The pooled former-drinker relative risk, the former-drinker to lifetime-abstainer ratio and the studies that were converted are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Publication bias tests gave no significant asymmetry: women Begg–Mazumdar P = 0.837 and Egger P = 0.215; men 0.767 and 0.196.

Continuous models: of eight first-degree fractional polynomials, power 0.5 fitted best in women (deviance 76.12 lower than the linear model) and the linear model fitted best in men; marked heterogeneity remained (women Q = 200.59, P ≤ 0.001, I² 72%, 95% CI 63–78%; men Q = 305.22, I² 78%, 72–82%). An interaction between dose and end-point (mortality against morbidity) was significant in women (χ² 7.89, 1 df, P = 0.005) and men (χ² 17.06, 1 df, P ≤ 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The fractional polynomials were restricted to monotonic forms on biological grounds (p. 439), so the continuous model cannot show a threshold or a dip; only the categorical model can.

key_findings.finding: Continuous model, women against lifetime-abstaining women: in mortality studies the relative risk of cirrhosis was 4.9 (95% CI 4.0–6.2) at 24 g a day and 12.5 (8.8–17.7) at 60 g a day; in morbidity studies 3.2 (2.6–3.9) and 6.2 (4.4–8.7). Men showed a similar, less pronounced pattern; men's values are given only as curves.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Figure 2 shows the fitted curves from 0 to 120 g a day without confidence bands or study points; values were not read from it.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Figure 2 viewed on the rendered page, values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Categorical model, women against lifetime-abstaining women (grams of alcohol a day). Mortality: >0–12 g 1.9 (95% CI 1.1–3.1); >12–24 g 5.6 (4.5–6.9); >24–36 g 7.7 (6.3–9.5); >36–48 g 10.1 (7.5–13.5); >48–60 g 14.7 (11.0–19.6); >60 g 22.7 (17.2–30.1). Morbidity: 0.4 (0.1–1.2), P = 0.105; 1.0 (0.5–1.9), P = 0.981; 2.4 (1.8–3.2); 1.9 (1.4–2.6); 5.9 (3.7–9.3); 6.1 (4.6–8.0). Mortality against morbidity interaction P = 0.023 in the lowest category and 0.001 or less in the others.
key_findings.note: Women's morbidity risk is lower at >36–48 g than at >24–36 g (1.9 against 2.4), so the morbidity series is not monotonic.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Categorical model, men against lifetime-abstaining men (grams a day). Mortality: >0–12 g 1.0 (95% CI 0.6–1.6), P = 0.991; >12–24 g 1.6 (1.4–2.0); >24–36 g 2.8 (2.3–3.4); >36–48 g 5.6 (4.5–7.0); >48–60 g 7.0 (5.8–8.5); >60 g 14 (11.7–16.7). Morbidity: 0.3 (0.1–0.9), P = 0.026; 0.3 (0.2–0.4), P < 0.001; 0.7 (0.5–1.0), P = 0.029; 2.0 (1.5–2.7); 2.3 (1.7–3.2); 5.0 (3.9–6.4). Mortality against morbidity interaction P = 0.05 in the lowest category and below 0.001 in the others.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Thresholds as the authors read them: in women's morbidity studies one to two drinks a day carried the same risk as lifetime abstention (RR 1.0, 0.5–1.9) and two to three drinks was the lowest category with a raised risk (2.4, 1.8–3.2); men drinking one to two drinks a day in morbidity studies had a lower risk than lifetime abstainers (0.3, 0.2–0.4), described in the limitations as a protective effect with no biological pathway; in women's mortality studies risk was raised from one drink a day on average. The authors conclude the results point to a threshold for morbidity but not mortality.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 6th paragraph (p. 441); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 442); Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph (p. 443)
key_findings.note: The text says men in mortality studies showed a similar dose threshold (p. 441), but in Table 2 their risk is already raised at >12–24 g a day (1.6, 1.4–2.0), one category lower than women's morbidity threshold; the discussion says a very low threshold could not be discounted for men (p. 442).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Sex difference as reported: women had higher relative risks than men at the same intake in both end-points; for five drinks a day (>48–60 g) in mortality studies, 14.7 (11.0–19.6) in women against 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men; the difference was smaller in morbidity studies. No statistical test of the sex difference is reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 5th paragraph (p. 441); Table 2, >48–60 g rows (p. 442)
key_findings.note: Each sex's relative risk is against lifetime abstainers of the same sex, so a larger relative risk in women does not by itself show a larger absolute risk; three of the studies contributed identical combined-sex results to both sexes (p. 439). Editors' comparison of Table 2: the women's and men's 95% CIs do not overlap at 8 of the 12 levels (all five mortality levels above 12 g a day; morbidity >12–24, >24–36 and >48–60 g) and overlap at four (mortality >0–12 g; morbidity >0–12, >36–48 and >60 g); the men's estimate is higher only at morbidity >36–48 g (2.0 against 1.9). Non-overlap is not a test, and the two sexes' estimates draw on partly different studies.

key_findings.finding: A sensitivity analysis comparing studies with sex- and end-point-specific ('pure') results with those whose combined results were entered in both datasets ('mixed') showed a very similar pattern; no numbers are given. The authors note that entering combined results in both datasets attenuates the differences.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Drinking pattern (binge drinking, drinking over time) and beverage type could not be analysed because the included studies lacked the information; the authors call for more data on regular light drinking and cirrhosis morbidity with former drinking assessed separately from lifetime abstention.

The authors' public-health reading: where cirrhosis is concerned "no alcohol consumption can be recommended", although up to two drinks a day may not raise the risk of morbidity, and people with any signs of liver problems should abstain.
key_findings.note: Quoted because the strength of the recommendation is at issue; it is the authors' advice, not a result of the analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled relative risk for former drinkers and the former-drinker to lifetime-abstainer ratio used to convert current-abstainer references to lifetime abstention are not reported, nor is the number of studies converted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the reference group is modelled rather than observed. Because the conversion raises the relative risks of every converted study by an unknown factor, the size of the correction behind each pooled estimate cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Results reported only for both sexes combined were entered in both the women's and the men's datasets, and results combined across end-points in both the mortality and the morbidity datasets. The text names the three studies without results by sex (refs 30, 36 and 40: Klatsky et al. 1981, Corrao et al. 1991, Bellentani et al. 1997), but Table 1 marks ten studies 'Both' in its sex column without separating them from the seven with results by sex, and the paper does not say whether the two Danish cohorts with end-point 'Both' (refs 39 and 44, Becker et al. 1996 and 2002) reported mortality and morbidity separately or combined.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex and end-point comparisons are not between independent sets of data, and the pooled estimates count some data twice; the authors' sensitivity analysis is reported without numbers.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that for all levels of consumption and both sexes the mortality relative risk was significantly higher than the morbidity relative risk (p. 441), but Table 2 gives an interaction P of 0.05 for men drinking >0–12 g a day.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the lowest category for men is at the conventional limit rather than clearly significant.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion explains a lack of difference between abstainers and drinking up to 12 g a day (p. 442, 2nd paragraph), but in Table 2 that category shows a raised mortality risk in women (1.9, 1.1–3.1) and a lowered morbidity risk in men (0.3, 0.1–0.9); only women's morbidity and men's mortality show no difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's summary of the lowest category does not match two of its four estimates; claims about light drinking must be taken from Table 2, by sex and end-point.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion's first paragraph says drinking up to two drinks a day was not associated with a significant increase in morbidity in women and men; for men the morbidity relative risks up to 36 g a day are significantly below 1 (0.3, 0.3 and 0.7), which the limitations call a protective effect without a biological pathway (p. 443) and which the abstract does not report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's 'indications for threshold effects' include statistically significant lower risks in men that the authors themselves find biologically implausible, a sign that the morbidity studies' reference groups or confounding may be distorting the low-intake estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 2 announces relative risks and meta-regression curves, but the figure shows only the fitted curves, without confidence bands or study estimates; Figure 1 gives exclusion counts without reasons.
reporting_issues.consequence: The curves cannot be checked against the data or their precision judged; only the text values for women at 24 and 60 g a day and Table 2 are citable.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2010_CirrhosisMA.pdf (all text read; Figures 1 and 2 viewed on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that end-point was an important source of heterogeneity (abstract and p. 443) is supported by a significant interaction term, but the heterogeneity remaining after end-point was added is not reported, and no heterogeneity statistics are given for the categorical model of Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: How much of the I² of 72% (women) and 78% (men) the end-point explains is unknown.
